Mozambique | RENAMO members contest UIR police presence at party headquarters

You are here:
  1. Home
  2. Politics
  3. Mozambique | RENAMO members contest…
Oct22026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:09
Instaread

Members of RENAMO are contesting the presence of the Rapid Intervention Unit (UIR) at party headquarters, calling for the withdrawal of the police force as a prerequisite for dialogue and for resolving internal rift that have divided Mozambique’s second-largest opposition force for months.

The position was presented today in Maputo by the coordinator of RENAMO’s Management Commission, Edgar Silva, during a press conference convened to announce the celebrations for October 4, National Peace and Reconciliation Day, and to express the group’s condemnation of the UIR presence at party premises.

According to Edgar Silva, the presence of the police force at various RENAMO headquarters creates obstacles to the normal conduct of party activities and hinders rapprochement between factions vying for control of the political organization.

“We did not take over the headquarters to vandalize anything; we are here to contest his leadership,” he stated, referring to RENAMO president Ossufo Momade.

The Management Commission official argued that the dissenting members seek to establish direct dialogue with the party leadership to find a way out of the internal crisis.

The challenge comes during a period of deep internal divisions within RENAMO, which intensified following the 2024 general elections and the dispute surrounding the leadership of Ossufo Momade.

Factions within the party have been questioning the management of the political force and demanding leadership changes, as well as meetings of internal governing bodies to discuss the party’s future and evaluate its electoral performance.

The crisis has also manifested through disputes over control of party facilities and clashes between opposing internal groups, creating a scenario that has severely disrupted the normal functioning of the organization.

The dissenting factions advocate for the removal of Ossufo Momade, arguing that a change in leadership could open space for the reunification of RENAMO’s various tendencies.

“RENAMO is sinking, and we are speaking out so that this does not happen again. The RENAMO family must unite,” stated Edgar Silva.

Edgar Silva also recalled an incident in 2025 when group members gathered at RENAMO’s national headquarters in Maputo to demand a meeting with party leadership.

According to the official, the gathering was dispersed by Police, who allegedly used tear gas and live ammunition.

“We were not armed, but they came and drove us away with live bullets and tear gas, even injuring our colleagues,” he claimed, alleging that some members suffered severe injuries.

The allegations presented by Edgar Silva were made during the press conference and were not immediately accompanied by a statement from the Police or RENAMO leadership regarding the reported events.

In addition to challenging Ossufo Momade’s leadership, members are advocating for an internal post-election review to determine the root causes of RENAMO’s results and assign accountability.

“We will request a review to find those responsible and hold individuals accountable for the debacle we experienced,” said Edgar Silva.

For the group, evaluating electoral performance must form part of a broader internal reorganization process, enabling the identification of systemic problems affecting the party and creating conditions for its reunification.

Conducting a review and opening a process of dialogue are presented as necessary measures to overcome the current crisis and restore internal cohesion to the political organization.

The protest was voiced within the context of celebrations for October 4, National Peace and Reconciliation Day, which marks the signing of the Rome General Peace Accords in 1992.

The accord was signed by the Government of Mozambique and RENAMO, formally ending 16 years of civil war and paving the way for the transition to a multiparty political system. The country’s first multiparty elections were held in 1994.

Invoking the peace process, dissenting members argue that the same principle of dialogue that made it possible to end the armed conflict should continue to guide the resolution of current political differences.

For Edgar Silva, the priority now is to prevent the worsening of divisions and create conditions for RENAMO’s various currents to find common ground.

The withdrawal of the UIR from party premises is, according to the group, one of the conditions required to facilitate this process and allow internal disputes to be resolved through RENAMO’s internal political mechanisms.

Source: AIM
